questions.title: Question 1: Linear search (12 marks)
questions.prompt: (a) Give the outcome and the number of comparisons of linear search for 18 and for 31 in `63 29 85 72 18 42 23 54 8 32`. (b) For 18 and for 31 in the ordered array `8 18 23 29 34 42 54 63 72 85`, stopping when an element larger than the key is seen. (c) State the best and worst cases of linear search. (d) Convert `for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) { if (arr[i] == key) return i; } return -1;` into a recursive method. (12 marks)

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: 18 is found at index 4 after 5 comparisons; 31 is not found, so all 10 elements are compared and the result is -1. (3 marks)

steps.title: Part (b)
steps.body: 18 is found at index 1 after 2 comparisons; for 31 the search stops at 34, the first element larger than 31, after 5 comparisons (8, 18, 23, 29, 34), and returns -1. (3 marks)

steps.title: Part (c)
steps.body: Best case O(1): the key is at index 0. Worst case O(n): the key is at index n - 1 or is not in the array. (2 marks)

steps.title: Part (d)
steps.body: `linearSearchRec(int[] arr, int key, int i) { if (i == arr.length) return -1; if (arr[i] == key) return i; return linearSearchRec(arr, key, i + 1); }`, called with `i = 0`. The first line is the end of the loop (not found), the second is the body, and the call with `i + 1` is the next iteration. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** 5 and 10 comparisons; 2 and 5 comparisons on the ordered array; O(1) and O(n).

questions.title: Question 2: Binary search (14 marks)
questions.prompt: (a) State what binary search requires and its best, average and worst cases. (b) Trace the lecture's method for 31 in `8 18 23 29 34 42 54 63 72 85`: give `low`, `high` and `mid` for each pass and the result. (c) Say what happens on the unsorted array `63 29 85 72 18 42 23 54 8 32` when searching for 29. (d) Name the bug in each: `while (low < high)`; `high = arr.length`; `low = mid`. (14 marks)

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: It requires a sorted collection. Best case O(1) (the key is the middle element); average and worst cases O(log n), because the search space is halved at each step. (3 marks)

steps.title: Part (b)
steps.body: Pass 1: low 0, high 9, mid 4 (34 > 31), high = 3. Pass 2: low 0, high 3, mid 1 (18 < 31), low = 2. Pass 3: low 2, high 3, mid 2 (23 < 31), low = 3. Pass 4: low 3, high 3, mid 3 (29 < 31), low = 4. Now low 4 > high 3: the loop ends and the method returns -1. (5 marks)

steps.title: Part (c)
steps.body: The method returns -1 although 29 is present (at index 1): it discards half of the array on the assumption that the array is ordered, which is false. Sort first. (3 marks)

steps.title: Part (d)
steps.body: `low < high` stops when one cell is left, so a key in that cell is never compared and -1 is returned (should be `<=`). `high = arr.length` is one past the last index: `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` for a key larger than every element (should be `arr.length - 1`). `low = mid` does not move past the rejected cell, so the loop may never end (should be `mid + 1`). (3 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** Four passes and -1 for 31; -1 on the unsorted array; `<=`, `length - 1`, `mid + 1`.

questions.title: Question 3: Lab 4 (8 marks)
questions.prompt: Lab 4 stores 50 random decimals in array 1 and the first 50 positive even integers in array 2. (a) Give the index of 2, 36 and 100 in array 2 and the result for 37 and 101. (b) Say why linear search for a typed decimal usually fails on array 1 and how to test it, and when the menu loop ends. (8 marks)

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: The value at index `i` is `2 * (i + 1)`, so 2 is at index 0, 36 at index 17 and 100 at index 49. 37 is odd and 101 is above every element, so binary search returns -1 for both. (4 marks)

steps.title: Part (b)
steps.body: `arr[i] == key` needs an exact match, and a random decimal will almost never equal a typed number; test by searching for a value taken from the array, and for one outside the range such as 80.5. The loop ends when the answer is neither `l`/`L` nor `b`/`B`. (4 marks)

questions.title: Question 4: Bubble, insertion and selection sort (14 marks)
questions.prompt: Sort `63 29 72 85 18` with each of the three algorithms and show the array at the end of each pass. State the number of comparisons of the lecture's bubble sort and of selection sort, and the number of items insertion sort moves. (14 marks)

steps.title: Bubble sort
steps.body: Pass 1: `29 63 72 18 85`; pass 2: `29 63 18 72 85`; pass 3: `29 18 63 72 85`; pass 4: `18 29 63 72 85`; pass 5 changes nothing. The lecture's version makes 5 passes of 4 comparisons: 20. (5 marks)

steps.title: Insertion sort
steps.body: After i = 1: `29 63 72 85 18`; i = 2 and i = 3 change nothing; after i = 4: `18 29 63 72 85`. It moves 5 items (1 for the 29, 4 for the 18). (5 marks)

steps.title: Selection sort
steps.body: After i = 0: `18 29 72 85 63`; i = 1: unchanged (29 is the smallest of the rest); i = 2: `18 29 63 85 72`; i = 3: `18 29 63 72 85`. It makes 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 comparisons. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** 20 comparisons (bubble), 5 moves (insertion), 10 comparisons (selection); all end at `18 29 63 72 85`.

questions.title: Question 5: Merge sort and merge (14 marks)
questions.prompt: (a) Sort `20 36 54 13` with merge sort, showing each division and merge. (b) Show the contents of `left` and `right` and the value written to each cell of `arr` for `merge(arr, 0, 2, 4)` on `{10, 40, 90, 20, 60}`. (c) How many merges does merge sort make for 8 items, and what is its time complexity? (14 marks)

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: Divide into `20 36` and `54 13`, then into single items. Merge `20` and `36` into `20 36`; merge `54` and `13` into `13 54`; merge those into `13 20 36 54`. (4 marks)

steps.title: Part (b)
steps.body: `size1 = 3`, `size2 = 2`: `left = {10, 40, 90}`, `right = {20, 60}`. 10 <= 20: `arr[0] = 10`; 40 > 20: `arr[1] = 20`; 40 <= 60: `arr[2] = 40`; 90 > 60: `arr[3] = 60`; the right copy is used up, so the rest of left is copied: `arr[4] = 90`. The result is `{10, 20, 40, 60, 90}`. (7 marks)

steps.title: Part (c)
steps.body: n - 1 = 7 merges for 8 items (4 + 2 + 1). The time complexity is O(n log n): about log n levels, each handling all n items once. (3 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** `13 20 36 54`; `10 20 40 60 90`; 7 merges and O(n log n).

questions.title: Question 6: Choosing an algorithm (10 marks)
questions.prompt: State the time complexities of bubble, insertion, selection and merge sort. Choose an algorithm and give a reason for: (a) 20 unsorted items searched once; (b) a million sorted items searched many times; (c) a nearly sorted list to sort; (d) a very large list to sort. (10 marks)

steps.title: Complexities
steps.body: Bubble sort, insertion sort and selection sort are O(n squared); merge sort is O(n log n). (2 marks)

steps.title: Searching
steps.body: (a) Linear search: the data is unsorted and small, so sorting first would cost more than the search. (b) Binary search: the data is sorted, and about 20 passes replace up to a million comparisons. (4 marks)

steps.title: Sorting
steps.body: (c) Insertion sort: it needs few moves on a nearly sorted list and has few overheads. (d) Merge sort: O(n log n) against O(n squared), at the cost of extra memory. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** Linear, binary, insertion and merge sort respectively.
